```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(here)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))

dat <- read.csv(here("data", "processed", "final_data.csv"))

regions <- read.table(here("data", "raw", "regions.txt"),
                      header = TRUE, sep = "", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
  select(iso = country_code, region, sub_region)

dat <- dat |>
  left_join(regions, by = "iso") |>
  mutate(exposure = factor(armedconflict,
                           levels = c(0, 1),
                           labels = c("No armed conflict", "Armed conflict")))

outcomes <- c(matmor = "Maternal mortality",
              infmor = "Infant mortality",
              neomor = "Neonatal mortality",
              un5mor = "Under 5 mortality")
```

This report explores `final_data.csv`, the analytical data set built in week 3
and verified against an independently written implementation in
`compare_final_data.qmd`. The aim is to understand the panel before fitting
anything: how complete it is, how the four mortality outcomes are distributed,
how common the conflict exposure is, and whether the unadjusted association
runs in the direction the paper reports.

# The shape of the panel

```{r}
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Rows", "Countries", "Years", "Rows per country",
               "Balanced panel"),
  Value = c(nrow(dat),
            n_distinct(dat$iso),
            paste(min(dat$year), "to", max(dat$year)),
            paste(range(table(dat$iso)), collapse = " to "),
            n_distinct(table(dat$iso)) == 1)
) |>
  kable(caption = "Panel structure")
```

Every country contributes exactly 20 rows, so the panel is balanced by
construction. That matters for the fixed effects models the paper uses: no
country is weighted more heavily simply because it has more years.

```{r}
dat |>
  filter(!is.na(region)) |>
  count(region, name = "Countries") |>
  mutate(Countries = Countries / 20) |>
  arrange(desc(Countries)) |>
  kable(caption = "Countries by region")
```

```{r}
sum(is.na(dat$region))
```

Every country matched a region, so the region labels can be used to stratify
without losing anyone.

# Missing data

Missingness is the first thing to look at, because a fixed effects model drops
a country-year when any variable in it is missing.

```{r}
dat |>
  select(matmor, infmor, neomor, un5mor, armedconflict, armedconflict_lag1,
         earthquake, drought, gdp_1000, oecd, pop_dens, urban, age_dep,
         male_edu, temp, rainfall_1000) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable",
               values_to = "Missing country-years") |>
  mutate(Percent = round(100 * `Missing country-years` / nrow(dat), 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(`Missing country-years`)) |>
  kable(caption = "Missing values by variable")
```

Three patterns stand out.

The 186 missing values of `armedconflict_lag1` are structural: they are the
year 2000 rows, where there is no previous year to lag. Any model using the
lagged exposure loses the first year of every country.

Several variables are missing exactly 20 times, which is one country missing
across all 20 years rather than scattered gaps.

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  summarise(across(c(infmor, neomor, un5mor, pop_dens, urban, male_edu, temp),
                   \(x) sum(is.na(x))), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(if_any(-iso, \(x) x == 20)) |>
  kable(caption = "Countries missing a variable in every year")
```

Maternal mortality is the real problem, with 426 missing country-years.

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  summarise(missing_matmor = sum(is.na(matmor)), .groups = "drop") |>
  count(missing_matmor, name = "Countries") |>
  rename(`Years of maternal mortality missing` = missing_matmor) |>
  kable(caption = "How maternal mortality missingness is distributed across countries")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(missing = sum(is.na(matmor)), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = missing)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey35") +
  labs(title = "Maternal mortality is missing for whole calendar years, not at random",
       x = NULL, y = "Countries with no maternal mortality value")
```

The pattern is not scattered. Almost every country is missing exactly two
years, and three countries are missing all twenty. The two missing years are
the same two calendar years for everyone, because the World Bank maternal
mortality series ends before the child mortality series does.

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(`Countries with a value` = sum(!is.na(matmor)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(year >= 2015) |>
  kable(caption = "Maternal mortality coverage in the last five years")
```

So a complete case analysis of maternal mortality is an analysis of 18 years
and 183 countries, not 20 and 186. The loss is systematic rather than random,
but it is also a clean truncation of the window rather than a pattern that
depends on conflict status.

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  summarise(any_matmor = any(!is.na(matmor)), .groups = "drop") |>
  count(any_matmor, name = "Countries") |>
  rename(`Has at least one maternal mortality value` = any_matmor) |>
  kable(caption = "Countries usable in a maternal mortality model")
```

# The four mortality outcomes

```{r}
dat |>
  select(all_of(names(outcomes))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(Outcome = recode(var, !!!outcomes)) |>
  summarise(N = n(),
            Min = round(min(value), 1),
            Q1 = round(quantile(value, 0.25), 1),
            Median = round(median(value), 1),
            Mean = round(mean(value), 1),
            Q3 = round(quantile(value, 0.75), 1),
            Max = round(max(value), 1),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(caption = "Distribution of each mortality outcome")
```

Every outcome has a mean well above its median, which is the signature of a
long right tail. Maternal mortality is the most extreme: the median is 66
deaths per 100,000 live births and the maximum is 2480.

```{r}
dat |>
  select(all_of(names(outcomes))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  mutate(Outcome = factor(recode(var, !!!outcomes), levels = outcomes)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey35") +
  facet_wrap(~Outcome, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "All four outcomes are strongly right skewed",
       x = NULL, y = "Country-years")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  select(all_of(names(outcomes))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value), value > 0) |>
  mutate(Outcome = factor(recode(var, !!!outcomes), levels = outcomes)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey35") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~Outcome, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "On a log scale the same outcomes are close to symmetric",
       x = "Log scale", y = "Country-years")
```

The log scale matters for how the models are specified. On the raw scale a
handful of very high mortality country-years would dominate the fit; on the log
scale the outcomes are roughly symmetric, which is why the paper models
them with a log transformation.

```{r}
dat |>
  select(all_of(names(outcomes))) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  round(3) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("Outcome") |>
  kable(caption = "Correlation between the four outcomes")
```

The three child mortality measures are almost the same variable measured three
ways, with correlations above 0.95. Maternal mortality is strongly but less
tightly related to them. Treating the four as four independent findings would
overstate how much evidence there is.

```{r}
dat |>
  select(all_of(names(outcomes)), year) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  mutate(Outcome = factor(recode(var, !!!outcomes), levels = outcomes)) |>
  group_by(Outcome, year) |>
  summarise(median = median(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = median)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~Outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Median mortality fell across the whole study period",
       x = NULL, y = "Median across countries")
```

Every outcome declines steadily from 2000 to 2019. A model that ignores
calendar time would attribute part of this global decline to whatever else
changed over the same period, which is why year effects belong in the model.

# The conflict exposure

```{r}
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Exposed country-years",
               "Percent of all country-years",
               "Countries ever exposed",
               "Countries never exposed",
               "Countries exposed in all 20 years"),
  Value = c(sum(dat$armedconflict),
            paste0(round(100 * mean(dat$armedconflict), 1), "%"),
            n_distinct(dat$iso[dat$armedconflict == 1]),
            n_distinct(dat$iso) - n_distinct(dat$iso[dat$armedconflict == 1]),
            sum(tapply(dat$armedconflict, dat$iso, sum) == 20))
) |>
  kable(caption = "How common the exposure is")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  summarise(years = sum(armedconflict), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey35") +
  labs(title = "Most countries are never exposed; a few are exposed almost every year",
       x = "Years of armed conflict out of 20", y = "Countries")
```

This distribution is the central limitation of the design. Half the countries
contribute no exposure variation at all, and a country fixed effects model
identifies the effect only from countries that change status during the window.

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  summarise(years = sum(armedconflict), .groups = "drop") |>
  summarise(`Never exposed` = sum(years == 0),
            `Changes status at least once` = sum(years > 0 & years < 20),
            `Always exposed` = sum(years == 20)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Group", values_to = "Countries") |>
  kable(caption = "Which countries can contribute to a within country comparison")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(exposed = sum(armedconflict), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = exposed)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  labs(title = "Number of countries in armed conflict rose over the study period",
       x = NULL, y = "Countries with 25 or more battle deaths")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  filter(!is.na(region)) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(`Country-years` = n(),
            Exposed = sum(armedconflict),
            Percent = round(100 * mean(armedconflict), 1),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(Percent)) |>
  kable(caption = "Exposure by region")
```

Exposure is concentrated in Africa and Asia, which are also the regions with
the highest mortality. The two are confounded at the region level, so a
comparison that pools countries would mostly be comparing regions rather than
measuring conflict.

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  summarise(transitions = sum(diff(armedconflict) != 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  count(transitions, name = "Countries") |>
  rename(`Changes in conflict status` = transitions) |>
  kable(caption = "How often countries switch conflict status")
```

# Exposure against the outcomes

```{r}
dat |>
  select(all_of(names(outcomes)), exposure) |>
  pivot_longer(-exposure, names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  mutate(Outcome = factor(recode(var, !!!outcomes), levels = outcomes)) |>
  group_by(Outcome, exposure) |>
  summarise(N = n(), Median = round(median(value), 1),
            Mean = round(mean(value), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(caption = "Each outcome by conflict status, unadjusted")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  select(all_of(names(outcomes)), exposure) |>
  pivot_longer(-exposure, names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value), value > 0) |>
  mutate(Outcome = factor(recode(var, !!!outcomes), levels = outcomes)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = exposure, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5, fill = "grey90") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~Outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Mortality is higher in conflict country-years before any adjustment",
       x = NULL, y = "Log scale")
```

The unadjusted gap runs in the direction the paper reports, and it is large:
median maternal mortality is several times higher in exposed country-years. But
this comparison is between countries, not within them, and the regional table
above shows how much of it could be geography rather than conflict.

```{r}
dat |>
  filter(!is.na(matmor)) |>
  group_by(year, exposure) |>
  summarise(median = median(matmor), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = median, colour = exposure, linetype = exposure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_grey(start = 0.1, end = 0.55) +
  labs(title = "Both groups improved, and the gap did not close",
       x = NULL, y = "Median maternal mortality", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
switchers <- dat |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  filter(sum(armedconflict) > 0, sum(armedconflict) < 20) |>
  ungroup()

switchers |>
  filter(!is.na(un5mor)) |>
  group_by(exposure) |>
  summarise(Countries = n_distinct(iso),
            `Country-years` = n(),
            `Median under 5 mortality` = round(median(un5mor), 1),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(caption = "Under 5 mortality within the countries that change status")
```

Restricting to the countries that actually change status is the closest this
EDA gets to the comparison a fixed effects model makes, and the difference is
far smaller than the pooled one. That is the expected direction: much of the
raw gap is between country differences that the fixed effects absorb.

# The covariates

```{r}
dat |>
  select(gdp_1000, pop_dens, urban, age_dep, male_edu, temp, rainfall_1000) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(N = n(),
            Median = round(median(value), 2),
            Mean = round(mean(value), 2),
            Min = round(min(value), 2),
            Max = round(max(value), 2),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(caption = "Continuous covariates")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  summarise(`OECD country-years` = sum(oecd),
            `Earthquake country-years` = sum(earthquake),
            `Drought country-years` = sum(drought)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Indicator", values_to = "Country-years") |>
  mutate(Percent = round(100 * `Country-years` / nrow(dat), 1)) |>
  kable(caption = "Binary covariates")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  filter(!is.na(gdp_1000), !is.na(un5mor)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_1000, y = un5mor)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "GDP per capita is the dominant predictor of child mortality",
       x = "GDP per capita in thousands, log scale",
       y = "Under 5 mortality, log scale")
```

```{r}
dat |>
  select(matmor, infmor, neomor, un5mor, gdp_1000, urban, age_dep, male_edu,
         pop_dens, temp, rainfall_1000) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  round(2) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(matmor, infmor, neomor, un5mor) |>
  rownames_to_column("Variable") |>
  kable(caption = "Correlation of each covariate with the four outcomes")
```

GDP per capita, male education and age dependency are all strongly related to
the outcomes, and they are also related to each other, so the adjusted
estimates will be sensitive to which of them the model includes.

# What this means for the analysis

The panel is balanced and complete enough to work with, but four things from
this EDA should shape the modelling.

Maternal mortality is missing for 426 country-years, and the pattern is
structural: the series ends two years before the child mortality series, and
three countries have no values at all. A maternal mortality model is fitted on
18 years and 183 countries while the child mortality models get 20 and 186, so
the two sets of estimates are not drawn from the same sample.

All four outcomes are strongly right skewed and close to symmetric on the log
scale, so they should enter the model logged.

All four outcomes fell steadily from 2000 to 2019, so calendar time has to be
in the model or the secular decline will contaminate the exposure estimate.

Only half the countries ever experience armed conflict, and the countries that
change status during the window are the only ones that contribute to a within
country comparison. The pooled gap between exposed and unexposed country-years
is much larger than the gap among those switchers, which is a warning that the
unadjusted contrast is mostly between country variation. The fixed effects
specification the paper uses is the right answer to that, and it is also why
the published effect sizes are far smaller than the raw comparison suggests.
